spots.name: Christ the Redeemer
spots.label: Christ the Redeemer

text.description:
Christ the Redeemer (Cristo Redentor) stands on the peak of Corcovado, a mountain about 700 metres high in Tijuca National Park, looking out over Rio de Janeiro. It is an Art Deco statue of Jesus with arms stretched wide, designed by Paul Landowski with Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa and built between 1922 and 1931. The figure is 30 metres tall, not counting its 8-metre pedestal, and the arms span 28 metres. It is made of reinforced concrete covered in soapstone, and it faces east.

It photographs well for a simple reason: the pose is instantly readable, and the statue sits high above the city, so the sky makes a clean backdrop. You can take a close, dramatic shot looking up from the platform, or turn round and photograph the view the statue is looking at.

Good to know: escalators, walkways and lifts were added in 2003 to help people reach the platform around the statue. A chapel under the statue was consecrated in 2006. Because the statue is so exposed to wind and lightning, it needs regular repair work, so scaffolding or restoration work is possible on some visits.

Allow time for the light and cloud to change. Take a few frames at different distances, from wide shots of the whole figure to close-ups of the hands and face.
text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for how to reach the summit and for any ticket or access rules.
text.geographic_location: At the top of Corcovado mountain in Tijuca National Park, looking down over the city of Rio de Janeiro.
text.directions_text: Start from central Rio de Janeiro and head for Corcovado mountain, which rises above the city. Escalators, walkways and lifts were installed in 2003 to help people reach the platform around the statue. Because arrangements for reaching the summit can change, check the official site before you go. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mornings are a good bet, as the statue faces east. Cloud can sit around the summit, so if the top is hidden, wait a little and check again.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out the stone. If cloud is passing, take a Live Photo or a few quick frames and pick the one with the clearest view. Wipe your lens first, as mist or fingerprints will soften the image.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the figure towers above you, so tilt the phone upwards and keep it level so the arms don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the body with the middle vertical line, so the outstretched arms are balanced left and right. Include some sky above the head. For a second kind of photo, turn round and use the default lens (1x) to capture the city and landscape the statue looks out over. Move a few steps to the side to keep other visitors out of the frame, or let a few people in to show how big the statue is.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the base, so the full height and the 28-metre arm span fit in the frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the statue with the city behind it. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the face and hands.

spots.name: Copacabana Beach
spots.label: Copacabana Beach

text.description: Copacabana is one of the most famous city beaches in the world, a four-kilometre curve of sand along the Atlantic shore in Rio's South Zone. It photographs well because the whole sweep of the bay can be seen at once, with Sugarloaf rising behind it. Along the sand runs the promenade, laid out with a black-and-white wave pattern in the Portuguese pavement style. That pattern dates from the 1930s, the promenade was rebuilt in 1970, and Roberto Burle Marx designed it. Historic forts stand at both ends of the beach. Fort Copacabana, built in 1914, is at the south end by lifeguard tower (Posto) Six. Fort Duque de Caxias, from 1779, is at the north end. The best long view is from the fort's outer wall, looking back along the sand towards Leme. Down on the beach itself, the wave-pattern pavement makes a good foreground line leading into the picture. Umbrellas and walkers add scale. On Sundays and holidays one side of Avenida Atlântica is closed to cars, so the beachfront feels more open. The beach also fills for big events such as the New Year's Eve fireworks, when an estimated two million people come. A weekday morning or late afternoon gives you more room and softer light. Check the fort's access before you set off, because it is a working army site.
text.access_note: Forte de Copacabana is a working army site with an entry fee, so bring photo ID and some cash, as cards may not be accepted, and check the official site before you go; the beach and promenade are open public space.
text.geographic_location: Copacabana Beach lies in the Copacabana neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro's South Zone, on the Atlantic shore. Leme is at its northern end, and Arpoador and Ipanema lie beyond its southern end.
text.directions_text: From the middle of the beach, the fort is about 2.3 km away, roughly a half-hour walk along the seafront, heading south. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early on a weekday or in late afternoon, when the light on Sugarloaf is at its best.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sand or the hills to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. Panorama mode works well along the parapet if you move slowly and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Forte de Copacabana (seaward parapet and the walk along the outer wall, south end of the beach at Posto 6). The full crescent of the beach curving back toward Leme, with Sugarloaf rising behind it. From here the beach is to the north, and you look back along the sand towards Leme with Sugarloaf rising behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the curve of the shoreline on a diagonal, with a little of the parapet or wall in the corner for depth. Use the ultra-wide for the whole bay, then take a second shot at 2x or more to pick out Sugarloaf. For another angle, try the rocky bluff by Quiosque Mureta do Leme at the northern end, which gives a wide view along the whole beach. At Posto 6 you can try a sunrise shot over the Atlantic.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the full crescent of sand. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Sugarloaf closer.

spots.name: Sugarloaf Mountain
spots.label: Sugarloaf Mountain

text.description: Sugarloaf is the granite peak at the mouth of Guanabara Bay that most people picture when they think of Rio. It rises 396 m straight from the water's edge. The Portuguese named it in the 16th century because it looked like the cone-shaped moulds used to carry blocks of refined sugar on ships. From Praia Vermelha, the beach at its south-west base, you look up at the rock rather than down from it, and that low angle makes the granite face look huge. The bay and the green hillside fill the sides of the frame, and the cable car often crosses overhead, which adds a sense of scale. That cable car opened in 1912, the first in Brazil, and the mountain is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site declared in 2012. The summit is a paid cable car stop and mostly photographs the city rather than the mountain, so the beach is the better place for the mountain itself. Guides suggest morning light, roughly 9am to 11am. Keep the whole rock in frame, with some sand or water in the foreground to lead the eye up. For a sunset alternative, try Mureta da Urca, where Sugarloaf sits behind the wall. For a long view with Christ the Redeemer and the city in the same picture, try Mirante Dona Marta.
text.access_note: Praia Vermelha is a public beach; the cable car and summit are ticketed, so check the official site before you go, and confirm access at Mirante Dona Marta before you go.
text.geographic_location: Sugarloaf stands on a peninsula at the mouth of Guanabara Bay in Rio de Janeiro. Praia Vermelha is the beach at the south-west foot of the mountain.
text.directions_text: Make for Praia Vermelha, the beach at the south-west base of Sugarloaf. Once you are on the sand, the mountain rises to the north-east. Drones are restricted around here, so leave them at home. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, about 9am to 11am, when guides say the light falls on the east face.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the rock to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale sky doesn't wash out the granite. Take a Live Photo if the cable car is moving, so you can pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (beach at the south-west base of the mountain). Sugarloaf rising straight above the beach, framed by the bay and the hillside vegetation, with the cable car crossing overhead. From here Sugarloaf rises straight above the beach to the north-east, framed by the bay and the hillside vegetation, with the cable car crossing overhead.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the beach or water in the lower third, with the peak rising above it. Tilt the phone slightly upwards, but keep it level so the sides don't lean. Wait for a cable car to pass if you want it in the shot. For a sunset version, try Mureta da Urca. Mirante Dona Marta gives a distant view across Botafogo and the bay.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole rock, the bay and the hillside in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the cable car against the granite.

spots.alt: Sugarloaf Mountain, Rio de Janeiro: the granite peak at the mouth of Guanabara Bay. Photo spot
